title: Spiral Survey
statement: A drone surveys a rectangular field of plots, recorded in matrix as rows of readings. It starts at the top-left plot and flies clockwise around the outside edge, then the next ring inward, and so on, visiting every plot exactly once. Return the readings in the order the drone visits them.

examples.explanation: Around the edge 1 2 3 6 9 8 7 4, then the center 5.
A wide field: the inner ring is the single row 6, 7.

hints.content: Simulating the drone with a direction and a visited grid works.
You can avoid the visited grid by tracking the four edges of the unvisited rectangle: top, bottom, left, right.
One ring: top row left→right, right column downward, bottom row right→left, left column upward. Then shrink all four edges.
Watch the last ring when it is a single row or a single column; it must not be read twice.
Only walk the bottom row if top < bottom, and only walk the left column if left < right.

testCases.explanation: Around the edge 1 2 3 6 9 8 7 4, then the center 5.
A wide field: the inner ring is the single row 6, 7.
A single row is read left to right.
A single column is read top to bottom.
A tall field whose inner ring is a single column.

solutions.title: Simulate with a visited set
solutions.intuition: Fly straight and turn right whenever the next plot is outside the field or already visited.
solutions.approach: Keep a direction index over (right, down, left, up) and a visited set. Repeat rows × columns times.
solutions.pseudocode: r = c = d = 0; for k in 0..rows*cols-1: out.push(m[r][c]); mark; next = step(d); if blocked: d = (d+1) % 4; move
solutions.spaceComplexity: O(rows × cols) for the visited set
commonMistakes: Turning only at the field's edges and forgetting already-visited plots.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Direct simulation is easy to get right; it uses extra memory for the visited set.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.content: Fly right 1 2 3, turn, down 6 9, turn, left 8 7, turn, up 4.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: Turn right into 5; every plot is visited.

solutions.title: Shrinking boundaries
solutions.intuition: The unvisited plots always form a rectangle, so four indices describe all the state.
solutions.approach: While top <= bottom and left <= right, read the top row, the right column, the bottom row (if top < bottom) and the left column (if left < right), then move every boundary inward.
commonMistakes: Omitting the top < bottom or left < right checks, which reads a lone row or column twice.
Starting the right column at top instead of top + 1, which repeats a corner.
solutions.interviewExplanation: The unvisited region is always a rectangle, so I keep four boundaries and peel one ring at a time. Each plot is read once with constant extra memory. The only subtle part is the final ring when it's a single row or column, which the two guards handle.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: Boundaries shrink to the center: top = bottom = left = right = 1 → 5.
